lessons.title: Why wireless is different: a medium anyone in range can hear

blocks.md:
On a wired network an attacker has to get a cable into a port. On a wireless network the signal leaves the building by itself. Every frame your laptop sends is a radio transmission, and any receiver in range hears it, wanted or not. That one fact, a **shared medium**, explains most of this course: Wi-Fi security is mostly about making overheard frames useless and forged frames detectable.

A tiny example: Ana sits in a cafe and joins the network `CafeLab`. Bo sits in a car outside with a laptop. Bo does not need to join anything to receive Ana's frames; the radio waves reach the car anyway. Whether Bo can *read* them depends entirely on the encryption, which is what lessons 2 to 7 are about.

Some vocabulary first. **Wi-Fi** is the Wi-Fi Alliance's brand for products that implement **IEEE 802.11**, the wireless LAN standard from the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers). The pieces:

- An **access point** (AP) is the base station that bridges radio clients onto the wired network. A client device is called a **station** (STA) in the standard.
- The **SSID** (service set identifier) is the network's human-readable name, such as `CafeLab`. The **BSSID** (basic service set identifier) is the MAC address of one AP radio, so one SSID served by five APs has five BSSIDs.
- Frames come in three kinds: **data** frames carry your traffic, **management** frames run the network (beacons that announce an SSID, association, deauthentication), and **control** frames handle the radio channel.

**Monitor mode.** A normal Wi-Fi adapter filters what it hands to the operating system: frames addressed to this machine, plus broadcasts. The Wireshark project's [WLAN capture guide](https://wiki.wireshark.org/CaptureSetup/WLAN) explains that to see other stations' traffic, or management and control frames, the adapter must be put into **monitor mode** (also called rfmon mode), which switches that filter off and delivers every frame the radio receives. Defenders use the same mode in wireless sensors and site surveys.

The consequence for defence is stark. NIST SP 800-153 (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology's guide to securing wireless LANs) notes that **passive attacks** only listen and transmit nothing, so "there is nothing for an organization to monitor electronically". You cannot detect eavesdropping; you can only make it pointless.

**How far does the signal go?** Further than the walls suggest, and the listener decides. Radio engineers reason in **decibels** (dB, a logarithmic scale where each 10 dB is a factor of 10 in power). Power is given in **dBm** (decibels relative to one milliwatt, so 20 dBm is 100 mW) and antenna gain in **dBi** (decibels relative to an ideal antenna that radiates equally in every direction). The transmitter's power, plus antenna gains, minus the **path loss** along the way, gives the received power. In empty space the loss follows the free-space formula in ITU-R Recommendation [P.525](https://www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-P.525/en) (the International Telecommunication Union's radio standard): it grows by 6 dB every time the distance doubles. An attacker cannot change your transmitter, but they can add receive gain with a directional antenna, and every dB of gain buys distance.

blocks.caption: Free-space path loss from ITU-R P.525. Received power in dBm = transmit power + antenna gains - loss.

Run with Python 3. Assumptions stated in the code: 20 dBm transmitter on channel 6 (2437 MHz), a receiver that can decode down to -90 dBm. Free space is an upper bound; walls and bodies cut real range sharply, but the gain still adds directly.

blocks.title: Received signal vs distance, and what antenna gain buys

scenes.caption: With a laptop's ordinary antenna (0 dBi here) the free-space signal stays above the assumed -90 dBm decode limit out to about 3 km. Real buildings absorb much of that.
A 15 dBi directional antenna lifts the whole curve by 15 dB. The crossing point moves out by a factor of about 5.6 (10 to the power 15/20). The defender did nothing different.
Takeaway: your network's reach is set by the best receiver in the area, not by where your office walls are.

blocks.md: **Two things that are not security.** In 2001 William Arbaugh and colleagues at the University of Maryland showed, in [Your 802.11 Wireless Network has No Clothes](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~waa/wireless.pdf), that "closed" networks fail because management messages carry the SSID in the clear, and that MAC address allow-lists fail because MAC addresses "MUST appear in the clear even when WEP is enabled", so an attacker sniffs a permitted address and uses it. Hiding the SSID and filtering MACs are still common advice; neither survives a listener in monitor mode.

Wireless security starts from one assumption: an attacker in radio range receives every frame, and can transmit frames of their own. Only cryptography (encryption plus authentication of every frame and of the network itself) changes what they can do with that position.

blocks.question: Your office network hides its SSID and allows only a list of known MAC addresses. A visitor in the car park runs a laptop in monitor mode. What do these two controls stop?
options: Both stop the visitor from joining, because the SSID is secret
Neither: the SSID appears in management frames from legitimate clients and permitted MAC addresses travel in the clear, ready to be copied
MAC filtering stops them, hiding the SSID does not
They stop eavesdropping but not joining
blocks.explain: Arbaugh and colleagues showed both fail against a passive listener: clients reveal the SSID when they associate, and every frame carries source MAC addresses unencrypted. Use real authentication (WPA3 or 802.1X) instead.

blocks.question: Why can't a wireless intrusion detection system alert on someone quietly recording your Wi-Fi traffic?
options: Because a passive receiver transmits nothing, so there is no signal to detect
It can: every receiver sends an acknowledgement
Because recording requires joining the network first
Because monitor mode is illegal
blocks.explain: NIST SP 800-153 makes this point: passive attacks only intercept radio transmissions, so there is nothing to monitor. Defences against eavesdropping are cryptographic, not detective.

lessons.title: WEP: how a 24-bit IV broke Wi-Fi's first encryption

blocks.md:
The original 802.11 standard (1997) protected data with **WEP**, Wired Equivalent Privacy: the name states the goal, privacy equal to a cable. It failed so completely that its failure is the best introduction to why every later design looks the way it does.

WEP used **RC4**, a **stream cipher**: it turns a key into a long pseudorandom **keystream** and combines it with the plaintext using **XOR** (exclusive or: an output bit is 1 when the two input bits differ, so XORing the same keystream in a second time removes it again). Every station on the network shared one secret WEP key, 40 bits in the standard (104 bits in common vendor extensions). Because a stream cipher must never reuse a keystream, WEP added a per-frame **initialization vector** (IV): a 24-bit value sent in the clear and prepended to the secret key to form the RC4 key for that frame. NIST SP 800-97 sums it up: "a 104-bit WEP key with a 24-bit IV becomes a 128-bit RC4 key".

**Flaw 1: 24 bits are too few.** There are only $2^{24}$, about 16.8 million, IVs. Once an IV repeats, the keystream repeats, and (as with a reused one-time pad, the cipher that XORs a random key as long as the message and is unbreakable only if that key is never reused) XORing two ciphertexts cancels the keystream and leaves the XOR of the two plaintexts. Network traffic is full of predictable headers, so one known plaintext reveals the other. NIST SP 800-97 notes that a busy network exhausts a sequential IV space "in a few hours", and with random IVs the birthday paradox gives a 50% chance of a repeat after about $2^{12}$ frames.

blocks.code:
import math

IVS = 2 ** 24                      # WEP's IV is 24 bits

def p_repeat(frames):
    # birthday bound: chance that at least two random IVs are equal
    return 1 - math.exp(-frames * (frames - 1) / (2 * IVS))

for n in (1_000, 5_000, 10_000, 20_000):
    print(f"{n:>6} frames: {p_repeat(n):.3f}")
print("50% point:", round(math.sqrt(2 * math.log(2) * IVS)), "frames")
print("counter wraps after", round(IVS / 1000 / 3600, 1), "hours at 1,000 frames/s")

#   1000 frames: 0.029
#   5000 frames: 0.525
#  10000 frames: 0.949
#  20000 frames: 1.000
# 50% point: 4823 frames
# counter wraps after 4.7 hours at 1,000 frames/s
blocks.caption: Computed with Python 3. 4,823 frames is a few seconds of traffic on a busy network.

blocks.title: Same IV, same keystream: the XOR cancels it

scenes.caption: Toy bytes computed with Python (the keystream is made up, not real RC4 output). Frame 1 encrypts the ASCII text 'GET ' and frame 2 encrypts 'PUT ', both with the keystream for IV 7.
The listener never sees the keystream, but XORs the two ciphertexts it did capture. Because both used the same keystream, it cancels out: 7d XOR 6a = 17, and so on.

c1 XOR c2 equals p1 XOR p2, and zeros show where the plaintexts match. Guess p1 = 'GET ' (a common header) and XOR it in: out comes 'PUT ', plus the keystream for IV 7, enough to forge frames with that IV.

blocks.md:
**Flaw 2: the integrity check was not cryptographic.** WEP appended a CRC-32 checksum (cyclic redundancy check, an error-detecting code) and encrypted it. SP 800-97 explains why that fails: CRC-32 is linear, so an attacker knows which checksum bits flip when message bits flip, and "bit flipping survives the encryption process". Frames could be modified in flight without detection.

**Flaw 3: RC4's key schedule leaks the key.** In 2001 the cryptographers Scott Fluhrer, Itsik Mantin and Adi Shamir (the FMS attack) showed that with the public IV placed in front of the secret key, certain "weak" IVs make the first keystream byte leak key bytes. Adam Stubblefield, John Ioannidis and Aviel Rubin turned it into a [practical key recovery](https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss2002/using-fluhrer-mantin-and-shamir-attack-break-wep/) in 2002, and Erik Tews, Ralf-Philipp Weinmann and Andrei Pyshkin [recovered a 104-bit key](https://eprint.iacr.org/2007/120) from fewer than 40,000 frames in half of their runs, gathering the frames in under a minute.

A longer WEP key does not help. SP 800-97: the technique "has known flaws that are not mitigated by longer keys". The problems are the tiny IV, the linear checksum and RC4's key schedule, none of which depend on key length. If a device only supports WEP, treat its traffic as unencrypted and isolate it.

**Defender view.** Prevention is simple: no WEP and no TKIP (WEP's stopgap successor, lesson 3) anywhere. Detection: a wireless sensor or a site survey lists every BSSID and its security mode, and any WEP network is a finding. Response: replace or isolate the device on its own VLAN, behind a firewall, and run sensitive traffic over TLS or a VPN.

blocks.question: Two WEP frames are sent with the same IV and the same shared key. What does an eavesdropper gain by XORing the two ciphertexts?
options: The CRC-32 values of both frames, but nothing else
The shared WEP key directly
The XOR of the two plaintexts, because the identical keystreams cancel
Nothing, because the IV is encrypted
blocks.explain: Same IV plus same key means the same RC4 keystream. XORing the ciphertexts removes it and leaves p1 XOR p2; one guessed plaintext then reveals the other and the keystream itself.

blocks.question: A vendor offers 'WEP-256' with a 232-bit secret key. Does this fix WEP?
options: Partly: it fixes IV reuse but not bit flipping
No: the 24-bit IV still repeats, CRC-32 is still linear, and the key-schedule attacks still apply
Yes, as long as the IV is random
Yes, the key is now too long to brute force
blocks.explain: None of WEP's three structural flaws depend on the key length. NIST SP 800-97 says exactly this about longer WEP keys.

lessons.title: WPA2: from passphrase to PMK to the 4-way handshake

blocks.md:
While the IEEE wrote a proper fix (the **802.11i** amendment), the Wi-Fi Alliance, the industry group that certifies Wi-Fi products, published **WPA** (Wi-Fi Protected Access) in October 2002. Per NIST SP 800-97 it was a subset of the 802.11i draft designed to run on existing hardware; its cipher, **TKIP** (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol), still used RC4 but with per-packet keys and a real message integrity check. When 802.11i was ratified, the Alliance named compliant products **WPA2**. WPA2's cipher is **CCMP** (Counter Mode with CBC-MAC Protocol, CBC-MAC being an integrity tag computed with the cipher), built on **AES**, the Advanced Encryption Standard block cipher. CCMP is **authenticated encryption**: it hides each frame and attaches a tag that reveals any change to it.

WPA2 has two ways to get the shared starting secret. In **WPA2-Personal** (also called PSK, pre-shared key) everyone types the same passphrase. In **WPA2-Enterprise** each user logs in through 802.1X (lesson 5).

**Step 1: passphrase to PMK.** The root secret of a session is the **PMK** (Pairwise Master Key; pairwise because it belongs to one client and one AP). In PSK mode it comes straight from the passphrase. hostapd's configuration file (hostapd is the open-source AP software used by Linux and Android hotspots) says the passphrase is 8 to 63 characters and that "this conversion uses SSID so the PSK changes when ASCII passphrase is used and the SSID is changed". The mapping is **PBKDF2** (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2, a deliberately slow function that turns a password into a key by repeating a keyed hash many times), with HMAC-SHA1 (a keyed hash built on SHA-1), the SSID as the **salt** (an extra input, so one password gives different keys on different networks) and 4,096 iterations.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, time

def wpa2_pmk(passphrase: str, ssid: str) -> bytes:
    # IEEE 802.11 passphrase-to-PSK mapping (same call as wpa_passphrase.c):
    # PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA1, the SSID as salt, 4096 iterations, 32 bytes out
    return hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha1", passphrase.encode(), ssid.encode(), 4096, 32)

print(wpa2_pmk("password", "IEEE").hex())        # test vector in hostap's self-tests
print(wpa2_pmk("sunshine1", "CafeLab").hex())     # toy home network
print(wpa2_pmk("sunshine1", "CafeLab2").hex())    # same password, other SSID

n = 200
t = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(n):
    wpa2_pmk(f"guess{i}", "CafeLab")
per = (time.perf_counter() - t) / n
print(f"{per * 1000:.2f} ms per passphrase on one CPU core, about {1 / per:,.0f} per second")

# f42c6fc52df0ebef9ebb4b90b38a5f902e83fe1b135a70e23aed762e9710a12e
# 3d523aabde1cbd76bb2b378edc2e225464cf0db18ade2ac17d59be8d412b4c9b
# 882f0ba34935af1a3208a25260ca51aff9f6124e17e8f557107d6100dc628a99
# 0.54 ms per passphrase on one CPU core, about 1,867 per second
blocks.caption: Real output on the author's laptop (timing varies by machine). The first line matches the passphrase test vector in hostap's crypto module tests. Changing only the SSID gives a completely different PMK.

blocks.md: **Step 2: PMK to session keys.** Every client already shares the PMK with the AP in PSK mode, so the PMK is not used to encrypt traffic directly. Instead, each time a client joins, the two sides run the **4-way handshake** to derive a fresh **PTK** (Pairwise Transient Key, transient because it lasts one session). Each side contributes a 32-byte random number: the AP's **ANonce** (authenticator nonce) and the client's **SNonce** (supplicant nonce; in 802.1X terms the AP is the authenticator and the client the supplicant). The derivation, as documented in wpa_supplicant's source (`wpa_pmk_to_ptk`), is:

blocks.caption: AA and SPA are the AP's and client's MAC addresses, AN and SN the two nonces. PRF is a pseudorandom function built on HMAC. Sorting with min and max makes both sides compute the same input.

blocks.md: The PTK is then split three ways, per the KRACK paper by Mathy Vanhoef and Frank Piessens (KU Leuven): the **KCK** (Key Confirmation Key) computes a **MIC** (Message Integrity Check: a short tag computed from the message and a secret key, which nobody without the key can forge; cryptographers call it a message authentication code, a different MAC from a MAC address) on handshake messages; the **KEK** (Key Encryption Key) encrypts keys sent inside the handshake; the **TK** (Temporal Key) encrypts actual data frames with CCMP. Broadcast traffic uses a separate **GTK** (Group Temporal Key) that the AP hands to each client inside message 3. Every message carries a **replay counter** so old messages can be rejected.

blocks.title: The WPA2 4-way handshake

scenes.caption: Both sides already hold the PMK (from the passphrase, or from 802.1X in Enterprise mode). The AP starts: message 1 carries its fresh ANonce and replay counter r. It is the only message with no MIC.
The client now has both nonces and both MAC addresses, so it derives the PTK. It sends its SNonce, protected by a MIC computed with the new KCK. This proves to the AP that the client knows the PMK.
The AP derives the same PTK and checks the MIC. Message 3 proves the AP also knows the PMK (its own MIC) and delivers the GTK encrypted under the KEK. Replay counter is now r+1.
The client acknowledges with message 4 and installs the keys; the AP installs the PTK when message 4 arrives. Data frames are now encrypted with the TK under CCMP.

blocks.md: Messages 1 and 2 move the nonces; messages 3 and 4 deliver the group key and confirm the keys, which is also how the handshake protects against downgrades. The PMK itself never crosses the air, but everything else that goes into the PTK does.

blocks.prompt: Two people on the same WPA2-Personal network both know the passphrase. One of them records the other's 4-way handshake. Can they decrypt the other person's traffic?
blocks.reveal:
Yes. The PMK depends only on the passphrase and SSID, which both know. The other inputs to the PTK (two nonces and two MAC addresses) were sent in the clear in messages 1 and 2. So anyone holding the passphrase who captured the handshake can compute that session's PTK.

The Wireshark project's [decryption guide](https://wiki.wireshark.org/HowToDecrypt802.11) relies on exactly this: give it the passphrase and SSID, and it decrypts any session whose four handshake messages are in the capture. A shared passphrase means shared confidentiality among everyone who knows it. WPA3 changes this (lesson 6).

blocks.question: In WPA2-Personal, which inputs to a client's PTK travel over the air in the clear during the 4-way handshake?
options: Only the GTK
None; all are encrypted
Only the PMK
Both nonces and both MAC addresses
blocks.explain: The ANonce and SNonce are in messages 1 and 2, and MAC addresses are in every frame header. Only the PMK stays secret, which is why the strength of the passphrase is everything in PSK mode.

blocks.question: Why does the client's message 2 carry a MIC?
options: To prove to the AP that the client knows the PMK, using the KCK derived from it
To carry the GTK
To reset the replay counter
To encrypt the SNonce
blocks.explain: Only someone who knows the PMK can derive the right KCK and compute a MIC the AP will accept. That is the client's half of mutual authentication; message 3's MIC is the AP's half.

lessons.title: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing

blocks.md:
Lesson 3 ended with a worrying fact: in WPA2-Personal every input to the PTK except the passphrase is sent in the clear. Now turn that around. Someone who does *not* know the passphrase records one client joining. They now hold the SSID, both MAC addresses, both nonces, and message 2 with its MIC. The MIC is a yes or no answer to the question "was this the passphrase?", and they can ask it as often as they like, on their own computers, without talking to the network again.

This is **offline guessing**: the attacker holds something that can check a guess (a verifier) and tests guesses on their own hardware as fast as it allows, with no lockout and no log entry on your side. Stolen password hashes are attacked the same way.

blocks.title: One captured handshake becomes a guess-checking oracle

scenes.caption: Simplified concept view. One recorded join gives a listener the SSID, both MAC addresses, both nonces and message 2 with its MIC. Only the passphrase behind them is secret.
Each candidate passphrase must first pass through PBKDF2 with the SSID as salt and 4,096 iterations, the step from lesson 3 that is deliberately slow.
That candidate PMK, plus the recorded nonces and MAC addresses, gives a candidate PTK and its KCK, exactly as both real parties computed theirs.
The KCK recomputes message 2's MIC. A wrong passphrase gives a different MIC; the right one reproduces it. The recording answers yes or no to any guess.
The access point takes no part: no lockout, no log, no rate limit. Only the size of the passphrase space and the cost of each guess set how long this takes (next figure).

blocks.md:
How long does that take? It depends on only two numbers: how many passphrases are possible, and how fast the attacker tests them. The size of the space is measured in **bits of entropy**: a passphrase chosen uniformly at random from $N$ possibilities has $\log_2 N$ bits. Eight random digits give $10^8$, about 26.6 bits; eight random lowercase letters give $26^8$, about 37.6 bits; four words picked at random from a 7,776-word list ($6^5$, one word per five dice rolls) give about 51.7 bits; ten random letters and digits give about 59.5 bits.

The attacker's speed is the assumption you must state. Our one CPU core managed about 1,900 guesses per second. Graphics cards and rented clusters do far more; the plot lets you slide that number.

blocks.title: Days to try every passphrase, by entropy and attacker speed

scenes.caption: At 1,000 guesses per second (10^3, about one CPU core) 8 random digits fall in about 1.2 days and 8 random lowercase letters take about 6.6 years. Average time to success is half of these.
At an assumed 100,000 per second (10^5), 8 digits take 17 minutes and 8 lowercase letters 24 days. 4 random words still need over 1,000 years.
At an assumed 10 million per second (10^7) 8 lowercase letters fall in under 6 hours. 10 random letters and digits still need about 2,700 years. Each extra bit doubles the attacker's work.
Real passphrases are not random: people pick words, names and patterns, which attackers try first. A human-chosen 12-character phrase can sit far to the left of where its length suggests.

blocks.md:
**Why the SSID salt only half helps.** A salt stops one precomputed table (passwords and their derived keys, computed once in advance and reused against every target) from working against every network. But the WPA2 salt is the SSID, not a random value. Two networks with the same name and the same passphrase have the same PMK, so a table computed once for a very common network name works against every network that kept that name. Renaming the network from the factory default costs nothing and removes that shortcut.

**What PBKDF2's 4,096 iterations buy.** Each guess costs 4,096 HMAC computations instead of one. That is a constant factor fixed when the standard was written, while hardware keeps getting faster; it does not change the shape of the curve above.

**WPS skips the passphrase entirely.** Wi-Fi Protected Setup's PIN mode checks an 8-digit PIN in two halves and the last digit is a checksum, so [CERT/CC VU#723755](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/723755) counts at most 11,000 online tries, after which the AP hands over the network password. Turn WPS PIN off.

Changing the passphrase does not protect recordings already made: if an old passphrase is later guessed, every handshake recorded under it can be replayed into the PTK computation. With WPA2-Personal, the passphrase protects the past as well as the future.

**Defender view.**
- *Prevent:* use a long, randomly generated passphrase (NIST SP 800-97: it "must be a long and complex, possibly randomly generated" value), or better, move to WPA3-SAE (lesson 6), which removes the offline oracle, or to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise (lesson 5), where each user has their own credentials and session keys.
- *Detect:* you cannot see the recording itself, and sometimes there is nothing else to see: the 2018 [PMKID technique](https://hashcat.net/forum/thread-7717.html) gets a guess-checking value from a single frame that many APs send to anyone who starts to join, with no client and no disconnection. When an attacker does need a client's handshake, watch for bursts of disconnections that force clients to rejoin, and for unknown radios advertising your SSID (lesson 8).
- *Respond:* if a passphrase may be known outside its intended group, rotate it, and treat past traffic on that network as readable.

blocks.question: An attacker has recorded one WPA2-Personal handshake. Which defence actually slows their offline guessing?
options: Turning on the AP's lockout after 5 failed logins
Hiding the SSID
Having chosen a passphrase with many more bits of randomness
Rebooting the AP
blocks.explain: Offline guessing never touches the AP, so lockouts and reboots do nothing, and the SSID is already in the recording. Only the size of the space the passphrase was drawn from, and the per-guess cost, set the attacker's time.

blocks.question: Why is a network named after the router's factory default slightly easier to attack than a uniquely named one, even with the same passphrase strength?
options: Default names disable encryption
The SSID is the PBKDF2 salt, so work precomputed for that common name can be reused across all networks with that name
Default names use WEP
It is not; the SSID has no effect on the PMK
blocks.explain: The PMK depends on both passphrase and SSID. A shared SSID across many networks lets an attacker amortise precomputation, the problem salts were meant to prevent.

lessons.title: WPA2-Enterprise: 802.1X, EAP and the certificate check that matters

blocks.md:
Lesson 4's problem was one shared secret for everyone. **WPA2-Enterprise** (and WPA3-Enterprise) gives each user their own credentials and each session its own PMK. You met the machinery in network-attacks-defenses: **IEEE 802.1X** port-based access control, where the authenticator (here the AP) blocks a device until a **RADIUS** server says yes, and **EAP** (Extensible Authentication Protocol) carries the actual login method between the device and that server. On Wi-Fi, a successful EAP run produces key material that becomes the PMK, and then the same 4-way handshake from lesson 3 runs on top.

The EAP methods you will meet:
- **EAP-TLS**: both sides present certificates; no password at all.
- **PEAP** (Protected EAP) and **EAP-TTLS** (Tunneled TLS): the server presents a certificate, a TLS tunnel is built, and inside it the user sends a password-based login such as **MSCHAPv2** (Microsoft's challenge-response protocol, version 2).

**The pitfall: the client must check who it is talking to.** In PEAP and TTLS the *only* thing that authenticates the network to the user is the RADIUS server's certificate. A server proves who it is with a **certificate**: a signed statement binding its name to its public key. The signer is a **certification authority** (CA), an organisation the client already trusts to vouch for names, and operating systems ship with many CAs preinstalled. NIST SP 800-97 describes the trap: clients are commonly configured "to accept certificates signed by any certification authority" they trust, and many CAs are preinstalled. An attacker then sets up an AP with your SSID and a valid certificate from any of those CAs, and clients associate and hand over their login exchange. The wpa_supplicant documentation is blunter about the empty case: "If ca_cert and ca_path are not included, server certificate will not be verified. This is insecure".

The fix in SP 800-97 is two controls together: trust only the CA that signed your RADIUS certificate, and check the server's name.

blocks.title: PEAP without a server name check: the user logs in to the wrong server

scenes.caption: Simplified. An attacker in the lobby broadcasts SSID CorpNet with an 802.1X configuration, using a certificate from a public CA for a domain they own. The laptop's profile trusts any public CA and checks no name.
The laptop starts PEAP. The fake server presents its certificate. It chains to a trusted public CA, so a misconfigured client accepts it.

Inside a tunnel that ends at the attacker, the laptop runs its MSCHAPv2 exchange. The attacker records the challenge and response. Known MSCHAPv2 weaknesses let them recover Ana's credentials from it, however strong the password is.
Correct profile: trust only the company CA and require the name radius.corp.example. The fake certificate fails both checks and the laptop aborts before sending any credential.
At work, the real server presents radius.corp.example signed by the company CA. Checks pass, the login runs inside a tunnel to the right server, and a per-user PMK results.

blocks.code:
# Vulnerable: no CA and no server name, so the server certificate is not verified
network={
    ssid="CorpNet"
    key_mgmt=WPA-EAP
    eap=PEAP
    identity="ana@corp.example"
    password="correct horse battery staple"
    phase2="auth=MSCHAPV2"
}

# Fixed: certificates instead of a password, our CA only, exact server name,
# and protected management frames required
network={
    ssid="CorpNet"
    key_mgmt=WPA-EAP-SHA256
    ieee80211w=2
    eap=TLS
    identity="ana@corp.example"
    ca_cert="/etc/cert/corp-root-ca.pem"
    domain_match="radius.corp.example"
    client_cert="/etc/cert/ana.pem"
    private_key="/etc/cert/ana.key"
}
blocks.caption: wpa_supplicant.conf, the Linux and Android Wi-Fi client. ca_cert, domain_match (full-name match; domain_suffix_match allows subdomains) and ieee80211w are documented options. Laptops and phones expose the same two checks as 'CA certificate' and 'domain' fields, or through MDM profiles.

blocks.md:
**Why EAP-TLS is preferred.** With PEAP-MSCHAPv2 a misconfigured client hands the fake server its MSCHAPv2 exchange, and Microsoft's [2012 advisory](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securityadvisories/2012/2743314) warns that published tools turn captured MSCHAPv2 traffic into the user's credentials, so a strong password does not save it; with EAP-TLS the client proves itself with a private key that never leaves the device, so a fake server learns nothing reusable. Certificates need a PKI (public key infrastructure, the CA and the processes around it), which is why organisations usually issue them through device management (lesson 16).

**Defender view.** Push Wi-Fi profiles from MDM with the CA and server name pinned, so users never see a "trust this certificate?" prompt they could click through. On the RADIUS server, log every authentication with client MAC, user and AP; a user who authenticates successfully but whose laptop also appears in WIDS alerts near an unknown AP (lesson 8) is a lead worth following.

blocks.question: A company uses PEAP-MSCHAPv2. Laptops trust the operating system's whole CA store and have no server name configured. What can an attacker with a public certificate for their own domain do?
options: Stand up an AP with the company SSID and receive users' MSCHAPv2 exchanges inside a tunnel that ends at the attacker
Decrypt the company's past traffic
Only cause a denial of service
Nothing; PEAP encrypts everything
blocks.explain: The client accepts any certificate chaining to a trusted CA, so the TLS tunnel happily terminates at the attacker. NIST SP 800-97 describes this exact scenario and its fix: a specific CA plus a server name check.

blocks.question: Which two client settings together implement SP 800-97's advice for EAP server validation in wpa_supplicant?
options: identity and password
eap=MD5 and phase2
ssid and psk
ca_cert pointing to the company CA, and domain_match (or domain_suffix_match) naming the RADIUS server
blocks.explain: ca_cert limits trust to your CA; domain_match checks the certificate's name. Either alone leaves a gap: a CA alone accepts any certificate that CA issued, a name alone accepts any CA.

lessons.title: WPA3: SAE, protected management frames and Enhanced Open

blocks.md:
**WPA3** is the Wi-Fi Alliance's successor to WPA2 (a certification that, per the Dragonblood paper, mandates existing protocols rather than defining new ones). Its Personal mode replaces the PSK handshake's front end with **SAE**, Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: "equals" because there are no fixed client and server roles: RFC 7664 notes that either party may start the exchange and both may run it simultaneously. SAE is the Wi-Fi version of **Dragonfly**, a password-authenticated key exchange designed by Dan Harkins in 2008 and later published as RFC 7664.

The goal is in RFC 7664's definition of resistance to dictionary attack: "any advantage an adversary can gain must be directly related to the number of interactions she makes with an honest protocol participant and not through computation". In plain terms: a recording of an SAE exchange gives an eavesdropper nothing they can test guesses against. To try a password they must actually attempt a handshake with the AP, one guess per attempt, which the AP can see and rate-limit.

How, at concept level: each side mixes the password into a fresh elliptic-curve (computed with points on a mathematical curve, which allows short keys) **Diffie-Hellman** exchange ([named](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2631) after Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman: each party picks a random secret, sends a public value derived from it, and both compute the same shared key, which a listener cannot). Each run picks new random secrets, sends a **commit** (values derived from the password and those secrets), then a **confirm** proving it computed the same key. What crosses the air depends on random secrets the eavesdropper never sees, so a wrong guess cannot be checked against it. The resulting PMK is different for every connection. The Wireshark guide notes the practical consequence: in WPA3 "a different PMK is used for each connection in order to achieve forward secrecy", so knowing the password and capturing a handshake is no longer enough to decrypt it, unlike lesson 3's predict question.

blocks.title: What an eavesdropper can test: WPA2-PSK vs WPA3-SAE

scenes.caption: WPA2-PSK: the PMK is a fixed function of passphrase and SSID, and the MIC on the air is keyed from it. That makes the recording a verifier.
The eavesdropper takes the recording home and tests guesses at hardware speed, as in lesson 4.
WPA3-SAE: the password is folded into a Diffie-Hellman exchange with fresh secrets on both sides. The eavesdropper records the commit and confirm messages too.
But those messages cannot confirm or refute a guess without the secret random values. The only way to test a password is to run SAE with the real AP, one try at a time, visibly.

blocks.md:
**Dragonblood: implementations and transitions matter.** In April 2019 Mathy Vanhoef (then at NYU Abu Dhabi) and Eyal Ronen (Tel Aviv University) published [Dragonblood](https://wpa3.mathyvanhoef.com/). Two classes of problem:
- **Downgrade.** In **transition mode** an AP accepts both WPA3-SAE and WPA2-PSK with the same password, so older clients still work. An attacker can set up a WPA2-only rogue copy; WPA3-capable clients connect to it and leave a WPA2 handshake, which is guessable offline exactly as in lesson 4.
- **Side channels.** The original way of turning a password into a curve point, called **hunting and pecking** in RFC 7664 (it keeps trying candidate values until one lands on the curve), loops a password-dependent number of times, so timing and cache behaviour leak information that narrows the password. The paper's proposed design changes went into a new draft of the protocols; hostapd now offers a replacement password-to-element method called **hash-to-element** (H2E), selected with `sae_pwe`.

**PMF (Protected Management Frames, IEEE 802.11w).** 802.11i encrypted data frames but, as NIST SP 800-97 notes, "does not offer protection to control or management frames", so anyone could forge a deauthentication frame and knock a client off (and make it rejoin, producing a fresh handshake to record). PMF protects unicast management frames against eavesdropping and forgery, and broadcast ones against forgery. It does not cover beacons or the frames sent before keys exist, so it does not stop an evil twin. The Wi-Fi Alliance requires PMF on all WPA3 networks and for all new certified devices.

**OWE (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, RFC 8110), marketed as Wi-Fi Enhanced Open.** For cafes and airports with no password at all: client and AP run a Diffie-Hellman exchange during association, so each client gets its own encryption keys and a passive listener sees only ciphertext. RFC 8110 is explicit that it "provides encryption of the wireless medium but no authentication": it stops eavesdropping, not an evil twin (lesson 8).

blocks.code:
# hostapd.conf, WPA3 transition mode: old WPA2 clients still work, but a
# WPA2-only rogue copy can downgrade WPA3 clients (Dragonblood)
wpa=2
wpa_key_mgmt=WPA-PSK SAE
rsn_pairwise=CCMP
ieee80211w=1                # PMF optional
wpa_passphrase=use-a-long-random-passphrase

# WPA3-Personal only: SAE, PMF required, hash-to-element allowed
wpa=2
wpa_key_mgmt=SAE
rsn_pairwise=CCMP
ieee80211w=2                # PMF required
sae_pwe=2                   # 2 = both hunting-and-pecking and hash-to-element
sae_password=use-a-long-random-passphrase
transition_disable=0x01     # tell clients: stop accepting WPA2-PSK here
blocks.caption: Option names and meanings from hostapd's documented hostapd.conf. transition_disable bit 0 tells clients that have connected with SAE to disable WPA2-Personal for this network in future.

blocks.md: SAE moves password guessing from offline (unlimited, invisible) to online (one try per handshake, visible to the AP). PMF stops forged disconnections. OWE encrypts open networks but does not authenticate them. None of them makes a weak password strong against online guessing.

blocks.question: A network runs WPA3 transition mode (SAE and WPA2-PSK with the same password). What is the main residual risk Dragonblood identified?
options: Transition mode leaks the password in beacons
SAE can be decrypted passively
An attacker can lure WPA3-capable clients to a WPA2-only rogue network and record a handshake that allows offline guessing
PMF is disabled by WPA3
blocks.explain: Transition mode exists for backwards compatibility, and that compatibility is the attack: the WPA2 half reintroduces lesson 4's offline oracle. Moving to WPA3-only, or using transition_disable once all clients support SAE, closes it.

blocks.question: An airport switches its open Wi-Fi to OWE (Enhanced Open). Which threat does this remove?
options: Passive eavesdroppers reading other passengers' unencrypted traffic
Phishing pages on the captive portal
All man-in-the-middle attacks
An attacker running a fake 'Airport-Free' access point
blocks.explain: OWE gives each client its own keys from an unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange, which defeats passive listening. With no authentication, a client cannot tell the real AP from a fake one.

blocks.question: Why did attackers like forged deauthentication frames on WPA2 networks without PMF?
options: They decrypt data frames
They disconnect clients, which then rejoin and run a new 4-way handshake that a listener can record
They change the passphrase
They disable CCMP
blocks.explain: Without PMF, management frames are unauthenticated, so anyone can forge a disconnection. The rejoin produces a fresh handshake for offline guessing. PMF makes such forged frames detectable and ignored.

lessons.title: KRACK and FragAttacks: when the standard itself is wrong

blocks.md:
Lessons 3 to 6 were about guessing passwords. **KRACK** (Key Reinstallation Attacks), published by Mathy Vanhoef and Frank Piessens in October 2017, needed no password at all. Its target was the 4-way handshake's state machine, and it affected, in Vanhoef's words, "all modern protected Wi-Fi networks", personal and enterprise, WPA and WPA2, every cipher. The handshake had formal security proofs; the proofs did not model when keys get installed.

Authenticated ciphers like AES-CCMP and GCMP (Galois/Counter Mode Protocol, another AES-based Wi-Fi cipher) need a **nonce** (number used once) per message. Inside, they run AES in counter mode, which turns key plus nonce into a keystream much like lesson 2's RC4, so reusing a nonce with the same key repeats the keystream. In WPA2 the nonce is a packet counter that starts at 1 when the TK is installed and increases with each frame.

**The bug.** Radio messages get lost, so the standard says the AP retransmits message 3 if it receives no message 4. The client, on receiving message 3, installs the PTK, and the CCS 2017 paper found that clients reinstall it each time message 3 arrives, which "reset[s] the incremental transmit packet number (nonce) and receive replay counter". An attacker who can delay frames (the paper uses a **channel-based man-in-the-middle**: they clone the AP on a different radio channel and relay frames between the two) blocks message 4, lets the AP retransmit message 3, and forwards it. The client reinstalls the same key with the counter back at 1, and starts reusing nonces.

wpa_supplicant 2.4 and later (and so Android 6.0 and later) had a worse variant: following a remark in the standard, it cleared the key from memory after installing it, so the reinstall installed an **all-zero key**.

blocks.title: KRACK against the 4-way handshake (simplified)

scenes.caption: The attacker relays the handshake between client and AP from a cloned AP on another channel, so they can choose which frames arrive. Messages 1 to 3 pass normally.
The client sends message 4 and installs the key. The attacker blocks message 4. The client starts sending encrypted data with nonces 1, 2, 3.
Having heard no message 4, the AP retransmits message 3 with a new replay counter, exactly as the standard says. The attacker forwards it.
The client reinstalls the same key and resets its packet counter to 1. Its next frames reuse nonces 1, 2, 3 with the same key: repeated keystream.
Patched clients refuse to reinstall a key that is already in use, so the counter keeps rising. The patch is backward compatible: messages and timing are unchanged.

blocks.title: The client's transmit nonce before and after reinstallation

scenes.caption: Frames A, B, C go out after the first install with nonces 1, 2, 3.
After the forced reinstall, frames D, E, F are encrypted under the same key with nonces 1, 2, 3 again.
A and D share a keystream, as do B and E. If A's content is known or guessable (many frames have predictable headers), D can be decrypted, just like WEP's IV reuse in lesson 2.

blocks.md: What KRACK did and did not do, from the disclosure site: it did not reveal the Wi-Fi password or the PTK; it let the attacker decrypt (and with TKIP or GCMP, forge) frames, replay frames, and hijack unencrypted TCP connections. "Changing the password of your Wi-Fi network does not prevent (or mitigate) the attack." The fix was software: install a key only once. Clients needed the patch for attacks on clients; APs needed it mainly if they supported fast roaming (802.11r) or acted as clients themselves. The coordinated advisory is [CERT/CC VU#228519](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/228519), with ten CVEs.

**FragAttacks** (fragmentation and aggregation attacks, Vanhoef, May 2021) found three more design flaws dating back to 1997, plus widespread implementation bugs. The design flaws: the flag saying a frame contains several aggregated frames was not authenticated (CVE-2020-24588); receivers would reassemble fragments decrypted under different keys (CVE-2020-24587); and fragments were not cleared from memory on reconnect (CVE-2020-24586). The site judged the design flaws hard to abuse; the bigger practical risk was implementation bugs such as devices accepting plaintext frames on a protected network.

Both disclosures make the same point about layering. KRACK's and FragAttacks' demos stole data only from connections that were not otherwise encrypted; the FragAttacks site notes that sites using HSTS (always-HTTPS, lesson 9) were protected. Wi-Fi encryption protects the hop to the AP. TLS protects the whole path. Design as if the Wi-Fi layer can fail.

**Defender view.** Prevention is patching, and the hard part is inventory: the FragAttacks site points out that smart-home and other internet-of-things devices "are rarely updated", and for them Wi-Fi security is the last line of defence. Keep a list of every Wi-Fi device and its firmware status, put devices that cannot be patched on an isolated network, and require TLS for everything sensitive. Detection is limited: a channel-based man-in-the-middle shows up to wireless sensors as a cloned BSSID on a second channel, which is lesson 8's rogue-AP detection.

blocks.question: After KRACK was announced, a home user changed their Wi-Fi password but did not update their phone. Are they protected?
options: No: KRACK never needed the password; the unpatched phone still reinstalls keys and reuses nonces
Yes, if the new password is long
Only if they also hid the SSID
Yes, the attacker now lacks the password
blocks.explain: The attack manipulates when an already-negotiated key gets installed. The password is irrelevant, as the KRACK FAQ says. Only patching the client's handshake logic fixes it.

blocks.question: Why does reinstalling an in-use key break CCMP's security, even though the key itself stays secret?
options: It disables the MIC
The reinstall reveals the key on the air
It resets the packet counter used as the nonce, so frames are encrypted under the same key and nonce again, repeating keystream
It downgrades CCMP to WEP
blocks.explain: CCMP (like any counter-mode scheme) is safe only while key and nonce pairs never repeat. Resetting the counter to 1 under the same key repeats them. It is the same keystream reuse that broke WEP in lesson 2.

lessons.title: Rogue access points, evil twins and how enterprises find them

blocks.md:
Two different threats share the label "fake access point":

- A **rogue AP** is an unauthorised access point attached to *your* wired network: an employee's travel router plugged into a desk port, or a device planted by an attacker. NIST SP 800-153 warns it "can provide a backdoor into the wired network, bypassing perimeter security mechanisms, such as firewalls".
- An **evil twin** is an attacker's AP that *imitates* your network (same SSID, sometimes the same BSSID) so that clients connect to it instead. It sits between the clients and the internet: the on-path position from network-attacks-defenses.

How easily clients fall for a twin depends on the security mode. Devices remember networks by name. For an **open** network any twin works. For **WPA2/WPA3-Personal** the twin must know the passphrase to complete the handshake, so a shared passphrase that leaks (posted on a wall, say) is enough. For **Enterprise** networks it works only against clients that skip server certificate validation (lesson 5).

blocks.title: Where fake access points sit, and where sensors see them

scenes.caption: Normal state: two inventoried APs serve CorpNet from the corporate LAN. Each radio has a known BSSID.
A rogue AP: someone plugs a travel router into a desk port. Anyone near it gets onto the LAN behind the firewall, whatever SSID it uses.
An evil twin outside the building advertises CorpNet with a stronger signal. A client that cannot tell them apart may roam to it.
Detection: a sensor in monitor mode hears every beacon and reports to the WIDS server. An unknown BSSID claiming CorpNet is an alert; so is a rogue device whose MAC shows up on a switch port.

blocks.md:
**WIDS and WIPS.** A **wireless intrusion detection system** (WIDS; with active blocking, a WIPS, and NIST writes WIDPS for both) uses sensors placed around a site that listen on all channels. SP 800-153 lists what continuous monitoring should detect: unauthorised devices including rogue APs; misconfigured devices or weak protocols; unusual usage (many failed joins, huge client counts); active scanning tools; denial of service ("a large number of events involving the termination of WLAN sessions"); and impersonation, such as a device spoofing another's identity. Sensors can also locate a threat by comparing its signal strength at several sensors, so someone can walk over and find it.

The core logic is a comparison against an inventory, which you can write yourself.

blocks.caption: Run with Python 3 on made-up sensor data. The second alert is a twin that copied a real BSSID but advertises an open network: the security mode gives it away. Real WIDS products add signal-strength location and wired-side checks.

blocks.md:
**Detecting rogue APs from the wired side.** A rogue AP often uses its own SSID, so SSID matching misses it. Wired signals help: a new MAC address appearing on an access port, a device answering DHCP that should not, or the same vendor MAC prefix seen both on a switch port and as a BSSID in the air. 802.1X on wired ports (network-attacks-defenses) stops an unknown router from getting onto the LAN at all.

**Response.** Locate the device with signal strength, remove it, and find out how it got there. SP 800-153 cautions against active scans of devices that might belong to someone else: identify and locate rather than attack. Never send forged frames against neighbouring networks; interfering with other people's radio networks can break the law.

An evil twin of an *open* network is indistinguishable from the real one at the Wi-Fi layer: there is nothing to authenticate. Users on open or OWE networks must rely on TLS (lesson 9) for everything that matters.

blocks.question: A sensor hears a BSSID that is in your inventory, but it now advertises CorpNet as an open network instead of WPA3-Enterprise. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The AP was upgraded
An attacker is spoofing that AP's BSSID to look legitimate, but cannot copy the Enterprise authentication
Normal roaming behaviour
A KRACK attack in progress
blocks.explain: Copying a MAC address is trivial; copying the RADIUS server's certificate and keys is not. A security-mode mismatch on a known BSSID is a classic impersonation signal.

blocks.question: An employee plugs a cheap travel router into their desk port to get better Wi-Fi, with its own SSID 'Jo-Hotspot' and WPA2-PSK. Which control would have stopped this from opening a path into the LAN?
options: Hiding the CorpNet SSID
OWE on the guest network
WPA3 on the corporate APs
802.1X on the wired access port, so an unauthenticated device gets no network access
blocks.explain: The rogue AP's risk is on the wired side: it bridges radio clients onto your LAN. Port-based authentication blocks unknown devices at the switch. WIDS would detect it; 802.1X prevents it.

lessons.title: Public Wi-Fi and captive portals in the HTTPS era

blocks.md:
"Never use public Wi-Fi" was sound advice when most sites used plain HTTP: anyone on the same open network could read and change pages. Today most traffic is HTTPS, which changes what a hostile hotspot can do. A precise picture of what remains is more useful than blanket fear.

First, the thing every hotel and airport network has: a **captive portal**, a network that, in RFC 8952's definition, limits access "until some requirements have been fulfilled", such as accepting terms or entering a room number, usually in a web page.

**How portals work, and why that is ugly.** RFC 8952 (Captive Portal Architecture, from the IETF, the Internet Engineering Task Force) states that current portals "typically implement some variations of forging DNS or HTTP responses", and some even attempt a man-in-the-middle proxy of HTTPS. In other words, the legitimate network behaves exactly like an attacker so it can show you its login page. Operating systems cope by fetching a known **canary URL** over plain HTTP when they join a network; if the answer is not the expected one, they assume a portal and open a mini browser.

RFC 8952 sets the requirement that new solutions "MUST NOT require the forging of responses", with the network instead advertising a portal API through DHCP or router advertisements ([RFC 8910](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8910)) served over HTTPS. Until that is universal, the habit "a certificate warning on public Wi-Fi is normal" is exactly what an attacker exploits.

blocks.title: Joining a hotspot: the portal, then HTTPS with HSTS

scenes.caption: The phone joins the open network and fetches the operating system's canary URL over plain HTTP to test for a portal.

The portal intercepts and answers with a redirect to its login page. The phone sees an unexpected answer and opens the portal window. This interception is the legitimate network behaving like an attacker.
The user accepts the terms and the hotspot lets traffic through. A hostile hotspot is now on-path for everything the phone sends.

The bank's site was visited before, so the browser remembers its HSTS policy and goes straight to HTTPS. The hotspot sees the server name and sizes, not the content, and cannot forge a valid certificate.

The remaining gap: a first visit typed as http://shop.example with no HSTS. That first request is plain HTTP, and a hostile hotspot can answer it with anything. HSTS preloading closes this for listed sites.

blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

<!-- for one year, the browser will only ever contact this host,
     and all its subdomains, over HTTPS -->
blocks.caption: An HTTPS response that sets HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security, RFC 6797). max-age is in seconds (one year here). RFC 6797 says browsers must ignore it if it arrives over plain HTTP, and should give users no option to click through certificate errors for such a host.

blocks.md:
**What a hostile hotspot can still do in the HTTPS era**, roughly in order of practical risk:
- Exploit the *first* plain-HTTP request to a site with no HSTS. RFC 6797 calls this the "Bootstrap MITM Vulnerability"; browsers mitigate it with built-in preload lists of HSTS sites.
- Phish through the portal page itself ("log in with your email account to get Wi-Fi").
- Attack apps that do not validate certificates properly (lesson 15). A browser warns; a buggy app may silently accept the attacker's certificate.
- See metadata: which IP addresses you contact, DNS queries unless encrypted DNS is used, and server names in TLS unless Encrypted Client Hello is used.
- Attack the device itself over the local network, for example through exposed services or wireless stack bugs (lessons 7 and 10).

**Defender view.** For users: prefer networks with real authentication; treat a certificate warning on public Wi-Fi as an attack, not a portal quirk; use a VPN where policy requires it. For organisations: HSTS with preload on every web property; managed devices that use encrypted DNS and an always-on VPN; and for the hotspot operator, OWE plus the RFC 8910 portal API.

On public Wi-Fi, TLS with correct certificate validation is what protects you, not the Wi-Fi layer. The risks that remain are the places where TLS is missing (first HTTP request, portal page) or broken (apps that skip validation).

blocks.question: A user on hotel Wi-Fi types `bank.example` (no https://) into a browser that has never visited it, and the site is not on the HSTS preload list. Where is the risk?
options: The first request goes out as plain HTTP, so a hostile network can answer it and keep the user on an attacker-controlled HTTP page
Only the DNS lookup is exposed
The bank's certificate will be stolen
None; the bank uses HTTPS
blocks.explain: This is RFC 6797's bootstrap MITM problem: HSTS only helps after the browser has seen the header over HTTPS, or if the site is preloaded. Preloading moves the protection to the very first visit.

blocks.question: Why do RFC 8952's authors want captive portals to stop forging DNS and HTTP responses?
options: Because portals need IPv6
It is slow
Because it makes the legitimate network indistinguishable from an attacker, breaks DNSSEC and non-browser apps, and trains users to accept interception
Because HTTP is deprecated
blocks.explain: The architecture's first requirement is that solutions must not require forging responses, and should let clients detect TLS interception without human exceptions. Interception by design teaches the wrong habit.

lessons.title: Bluetooth and BLE: pairing, KNOB and BlueBorne

blocks.md:
**Bluetooth** is named after Harald "Bluetooth" Gormsson, the tenth-century king who united Denmark and Norway; per the [Bluetooth SIG](https://www.bluetooth.com/about-us/bluetooth-origin/) (Special Interest Group, the body that runs the standard), Jim Kardach of Intel proposed it in 1996 as a placeholder code name because the project aimed to unite the PC and mobile industries, and the placeholder stuck. It is not an acronym.

There are two radio families. **BR/EDR** (Basic Rate / Enhanced Data Rate, often called Bluetooth Classic) carries headsets and car audio. **BLE** (Bluetooth Low Energy) carries fitness bands, locks, medical sensors and item trackers. Both are short range by design, but lesson 1's radio maths applies: a better antenna extends range.

Security starts with **pairing**: two devices that have never met create a shared long-term key. Everything later (encryption, reconnecting without asking) depends on how well pairing resisted eavesdroppers and men-in-the-middle.

NIST SP 800-121 (Guide to Bluetooth Security) describes the modern method, **Secure Simple Pairing** (SSP), which added elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) so that a passive eavesdropper cannot compute the key. SSP chooses an **association model** from what each device can display or type:
- **Numeric Comparison**: both screens show a six-digit number and the user confirms they match. Protects against a man-in-the-middle (MITM).
- **Passkey Entry**: one device shows six digits, the user types them on the other. Protects against MITM.
- **Just Works**: for devices with no screen or keyboard (a headset). Same exchange, but nobody compares anything, so "Just Works provides no MITM protection".
- **Out of Band** (OOB): keys are exchanged over another channel such as NFC (near-field communication, the tap-to-pair radio).

BLE's older **LE Legacy Pairing** was weaker: in its Just Works mode the temporary key is all zeros, so an eavesdropper "does not need to guess" it. **LE Secure Connections** (Bluetooth 4.2) brought ECDH to BLE, and a **Secure Connections Only** mode refuses anything older.

**KNOB (Key Negotiation of Bluetooth), 2019.** Daniele Antonioli (Singapore University of Technology and Design), Nils Ole Tippenhauer (CISPA) and Kasper Rasmussen (University of Oxford) looked past pairing to the next step. After two BR/EDR devices authenticate, their Bluetooth chips negotiate how many bytes of entropy the encryption key will have: any value from 1 to 16, as the specification allowed. The negotiation runs over **LMP** (Link Manager Protocol, chip-to-chip control messages) and is "neither encrypted nor authenticated", and the operating system above the chip never sees it. An attacker in range rewrites the proposals so both sides agree on **one byte**, then tries all 256 keys. It worked even with Secure Connections, and every device they tested was vulnerable: the paper lists more than 14 chips across 21 devices, all accepting a 1-byte key except Apple's W1 chip, which still accepted 7 bytes.

blocks.title: KNOB: rewriting the key-length negotiation

scenes.caption: Simplified. After pairing and authentication, the phone's Bluetooth chip proposes a 16-byte encryption key. LMP messages carry no integrity protection.
The attacker changes the proposal to 1 byte before it reaches the headset. 1 is within the specification's range, so the headset accepts.
Toward the phone, the attacker presents a counter-proposal of 1 byte, which looks like a limited headset. The phone accepts.
Both report 'encryption on' to their operating systems. The key has 256 possibilities; the attacker tries them all and decrypts or injects traffic.
The fix: the Bluetooth SIG now recommends, and tests for, a minimum of 7 bytes, and patched hosts reject anything shorter.

blocks.caption: Python 3. The rate is an assumption to make the comparison concrete. The SIG's 7-byte minimum is a floor that blocks KNOB's instant break, not a recommended strength; full 16-byte keys are the norm.

blocks.md: The SIG's [statement](https://www.bluetooth.com/security/statement-key-negotiation-of-bluetooth) updated the Core Specification "to recommend a minimum encryption key length of 7 octets for BR/EDR connections". The CERT/CC note is [VU#918987](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/918987) (CVE-2019-9506).

**BlueBorne, 2017.** Ben Seri and Gregory Vishnepolsky of the security firm Armis found eight vulnerabilities across the Bluetooth stacks of Android, Linux, Windows and iOS. Their white paper stresses two misconceptions: that Bluetooth connections need paired devices ("which they do not") and that a device's Bluetooth address is hidden when not discoverable ("which they are not"). The attack did not need the target to be discoverable or paired, or the user to approve anything. One example from CERT/CC's [VU#240311](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/240311): Linux's L2CAP configuration code (L2CAP, the Logical Link Control and Adaptation Protocol, is Bluetooth's packet multiplexing layer) did not check a length before unpacking, overflowing "a 64 byte buffer on the kernel stack" (CVE-2017-1000251). Bluetooth stacks run inside the kernel or as highly privileged processes, so a parser bug there is a remote path to full control.

Bluetooth has two separate risk classes. Protocol design (pairing models, KNOB's unauthenticated negotiation) decides what a nearby listener or MITM can do to a correct implementation. Implementation bugs (BlueBorne) let a nearby attacker run code, with no pairing at all. Updates fix both; turning Bluetooth off removes the second.

**Defender view.** Prevent: patch phones, laptops and especially embedded devices; prefer devices that support Secure Connections and use Numeric Comparison or Passkey Entry; turn Bluetooth off on servers and kiosks that do not need it; for high-assurance environments, Secure Connections Only mode. Detect: Bluetooth is rarely monitored, so inventory what is enabled, and where policy requires, survey for unexpected devices. Respond: when a stack bug like BlueBorne is announced, the exposure is every device with the radio on, which makes radio inventory part of patch triage.

blocks.question: A smart lock pairs with phones using BLE Legacy Pairing in Just Works mode. What can a passive eavesdropper who records the pairing do?
options: Nothing, BLE is always encrypted
Derive the keys, because Legacy Just Works uses an all-zero temporary key
Only learn the lock's name
Cause the lock to require Numeric Comparison
blocks.explain: NIST SP 800-121: in LE Legacy Pairing Just Works, the temporary key is zero, so an eavesdropper does not need to guess it. LE Secure Connections uses ECDH, which defeats passive eavesdroppers.

blocks.question: Why could the KNOB attack succeed even against devices using Bluetooth's strongest pairing mode?
options: Because the key-length negotiation happens later, between the chips, over unauthenticated LMP messages the OS never sees
Because the attacker knew the PIN
Because KNOB broke ECDH
Because Secure Connections uses short PINs
blocks.explain: Pairing was fine; the attacker shrank the *derived* encryption key's entropy afterwards. The fix enforces a minimum key length so a downgraded negotiation is rejected.

lessons.title: iOS: code signing, sandbox, Secure Enclave and BlastDoor

blocks.md:
The rest of the course moves from the radio to the device in your pocket. A phone holds more about a person than any laptop: messages, photos, location history, banking, health data, and the codes that unlock everything else. Its threat model is also unusual: it is always on, always connected, and constantly parsing data that strangers send it (messages, calls, images).

os-security-isolation already covered iOS sandboxing and entitlements at concept level. This lesson assembles the full iOS defence, using Apple's *Platform Security* guide, from the outside in.

**1. Only signed code runs.** iOS requires "that all executable code be signed using an Apple-issued certificate". Developers join the Apple Developer Program, Apple verifies their real-world identity, and App Store apps are reviewed. At launch, the system checks the signature of every dynamic library a process links against: an app may load only system libraries or libraries carrying its own 10-character **Team ID**. This stops an app from loading someone else's code into itself or modifying its own code at run time.

**2. Every app is sandboxed.** "All third-party apps are sandboxed": each gets a randomly assigned home directory, runs as the unprivileged user `mobile`, and reaches other apps' data only through services iOS provides. The operating system partition is mounted read-only. **Entitlements**, signed key-value pairs, grant specific capabilities, and because they are signed "they can't be changed".

**3. Memory protections.** Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) and ARM's Execute Never (XN) bit make memory-corruption bugs (code that reads or writes outside the memory it should, so crafted input can overwrite data the program relies on) harder to exploit; writable-and-executable memory requires an Apple-only entitlement (used by Safari's JavaScript compiler).

**4. The Secure Enclave.** A dedicated security subsystem inside Apple's chips, "isolated from the main processor" and "designed to keep sensitive user data secure even when the Application Processor kernel becomes compromised". It has its own processor (running an Apple-customised L4 microkernel), its own boot ROM, AES engine and random number generator, and encrypted, authenticated memory. Face ID and Touch ID data and the keys at the root of file encryption are protected there, not in iOS.

**5. Data Protection.** Every file gets its own 256-bit key, and each file belongs to a **protection class** that decides when its key is available: for example, only while unlocked, or after the first unlock since boot. In the strongest class, Complete Protection, the class key is protected by a key derived from the passcode and the device's hardware UID key, and the decrypted class key is discarded shortly after the device locks; a stolen, locked phone does not expose those files. Third-party apps "receive this protection automatically", and can choose a stricter class.

blocks.caption: Swift, type-checked with swiftc. .completeFileProtection maps to the NSFileProtectionComplete class from Apple's Data Protection table; lesson 14 does the same for secrets in the Keychain.

blocks.md: **6. BlastDoor: armour for the zero-click path.** Since iOS 14, "BlastDoor isolates, parses, transcodes, and validates untrusted data arriving in Messages" and Apple's identity services, using sandbox restrictions and memory-safe validation, specifically against "0-click" attacks. Samuel Gross of Google Project Zero (Google's team that hunts for unknown vulnerabilities in widely used software), who reverse engineered it in [A Look at iMessage in iOS 14](https://googleprojectzero.blogspot.com/2021/01/a-look-at-imessage-in-ios-14.html), found three changes: the new service is written mostly in Swift (memory-safe) and is the most tightly sandboxed step in the pipeline; the shared library region is re-randomised when an attack that probes it by crashing processes is detected; and crashed BlastDoor and imagent processes restart with exponentially growing delays, up to an apparent 20 minutes, turning a minutes-long brute force into hours.

blocks.title: The iMessage receive path after BlastDoor (simplified)

scenes.caption: A message from anyone who knows your number or Apple ID arrives through Apple's servers. Only a couple of processes in this chain (such as apsd) may use the network at all.
Complex, attacker-controlled content (serialized objects, link previews) is parsed in BlastDoor: memory-safe Swift, tight sandbox, crash throttling. A bug here should give the attacker very little.

Every extra parser outside BlastDoor is attack surface. In 2021 Project Zero found GIF handling went to IMTranscoderAgent, outside BlastDoor: the door FORCEDENTRY used (lesson 17). Apple later moved GIF decoding into BlastDoor.
Only validated, simplified results reach the user interface. The design goal: assume parsers have bugs, and make each bug worth as little as possible.

blocks.md: iOS security is layered: signed code only, every app sandboxed, entitlements signed in, memory mitigations, keys in a separate Secure Enclave, files encrypted per class, and the riskiest parsers isolated in BlastDoor. Real attacks (lesson 17) need a chain of bugs to get through several layers.

blocks.question: An attacker gains code execution inside the iOS kernel. According to Apple's design, what should still be protected?
options: Only App Store apps
Only files in the Documents folder
Nothing; the kernel controls everything
Keys held by the Secure Enclave, which is isolated from the application processor and designed for this case
blocks.explain: Apple's guide states the Secure Enclave is designed to keep sensitive data secure even when the Application Processor kernel is compromised. The attacker may use the device, but cannot extract keys that never leave the enclave.

blocks.question: Why did Apple add exponential restart throttling to BlastDoor and imagent?
options: Because Swift crashes more often
To save battery
Because many zero-click exploits need to crash a service many times (for example to break ASLR); doubling the restart delay stretches minutes into hours
To stop spam
blocks.explain: Project Zero's analysis: crash-oracle techniques learn memory layout by repeatedly crashing a service. With delays doubling up to about 20 minutes, such an exploit would need hours to roughly half a day.

lessons.title: Android: UID sandbox, SELinux, verified boot and Play Protect

blocks.md:
Android builds its sandbox from the oldest Unix mechanism there is. The AOSP (Android Open Source Project) documentation: "Android assigns a unique user ID (UID) to each Android app and runs it in its own process", and the kernel then enforces separation with ordinary user and group permissions. If app A tries to read app B's files, it fails exactly as one Linux user reading another's home directory would. Because the boundary is in the kernel, native code is "as sandboxed as interpreted code".

A tiny example: a notes app runs as UID 10123 and a game as UID 10187. The notes app's files live in its private data directory, owned by 10123 with mode 700 (owner only; the default for apps targeting Android 7.0 and later). The game's process, running as 10187, gets "permission denied".

Over the years Android stacked further layers onto that base, per the same AOSP page:
- **SELinux** (Security-Enhanced Linux, the mandatory access control system from os-security-isolation) has been enforcing since Android 5.0, by default-deny policy. Since Android 9, each non-privileged app that targets API level 28 or higher (the API level is Android's version number for developers; 28 is Android 9) gets its own SELinux sandbox, so even an app that tries to make its files world-readable cannot. Denials are logged to `dmesg` and `logcat`.
- **seccomp-bpf** (a system-call filter) has applied to all apps since Android 8.0, shrinking the kernel attack surface.
- **Scoped storage** (Android 10): apps no longer get a raw view of shared storage such as `/sdcard/DCIM`.

To share data, apps use a **content provider** (a component that serves data to other apps with checks), not world-readable files.

blocks.title: Layers between one Android app and another app's data

scenes.caption: The notes app reads its own private files freely: its process runs as their owner, UID 10123.
A compromised game (UID 10187) tries to open the notes file directly. The kernel's ordinary permission check fails first: wrong owner, mode 700.
Even if the file were made world-readable, SELinux would still deny it: each app has its own domain, and policy says no. The denial is logged.
To break out the attacker needs a kernel bug, reached through the system calls seccomp still allows. That is why real Android chains end with a kernel or driver exploit (lesson 17).
The legitimate path: ask a content provider, which checks the caller's permissions and shares only what it chooses.

blocks.md: **Verified Boot** ensures "all executed code comes from a trusted source", building a chain of trust from a hardware root through the bootloader to the boot, system and vendor partitions: each stage checks the next before running it. Since Android 7.0 it is strictly enforced, so a corrupted device will not boot, and **rollback protection** stops an attacker from installing an older, vulnerable version to make an exploit persistent.

**Google Play Protect** scans apps for PHAs (potentially harmful applications), on the device and in Google's cloud, including apps from outside Google Play, and works to prevent the installation of harmful apps. Enterprises can query a device's Play Protect status through the Play Integrity API.

**The Android update gap.** Unlike iOS, Android devices often get fixes through a chain: Google, component vendors (chips, codecs, drivers), then the phone maker. Each phone reports a **security patch level**, a date, and that date (not the Android version number) tells you which published bulletins are fixed. Lesson 17's Pixel case shows how long that chain can be.

Rooting a phone (gaining root, Unix's all-powerful user) or unlocking its bootloader deliberately removes layers described here: verified boot no longer vouches for the system, and root can override the UID sandbox. Fine for a lab device, a serious risk on one that holds work data; device management and attestation checks such as the Play Integrity API (lesson 16) let organisations detect it.

blocks.question: App A and app B on Android are both malicious and collude. App A makes its private files world-readable so B can read them. On an Android 13 device, where A targets API 33, what stops this?
options: The per-app SELinux sandbox for apps targeting API 28+, which prevents apps from making their data world-accessible
Play Protect deletes the files
Verified boot
Nothing; world-readable means everyone
blocks.explain: AOSP: since Android 9, non-privileged apps targeting API 28+ run in individual SELinux sandboxes, which 'prevents apps from making their data world accessible'. Mandatory access control overrides the owner's choice.

blocks.question: Why does verified boot include rollback protection?
options: To make updates faster
So that an attacker cannot reinstall an older, signed but vulnerable system image to exploit a bug that has since been fixed
To roll back bad updates automatically
To protect the user's photos
blocks.explain: Old images were validly signed too. Without rollback protection, signing alone would let an attacker downgrade to a version with a known exploit and make it persistent.

lessons.title: App permissions and the principle of least privilege

blocks.md:
The sandbox keeps apps apart. **Permissions** are how a sandboxed app is let back out, one capability at a time: the camera, the microphone, contacts, precise location. The principle behind good permission design is **least privilege** (from os-security-isolation: every component gets only the access it needs for its job, for as long as it needs it).

Apple's developer guidance puts it plainly: a navigation app needs location, but "doesn't need access to a person's health history, camera interface, or Bluetooth peripherals". iOS restricts protected resources by default; the first time an app touches one, the system shows a prompt with the app's **purpose string** (for the camera, the `NSCameraUsageDescription` key in Info.plist), and the user decides. For location, the user can choose "Allow Once".

Android sorts permissions by risk ([Permissions overview](https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/permissions/overview)):
- **Install-time** permissions, granted automatically: *normal* ones (little risk, such as internet access) and *signature* ones (granted only to apps signed with the same certificate as the app that defined them, used for privileged services).
- **Runtime** permissions, also called *dangerous*: access to private data such as location, contacts, microphone and camera. The app must ask, at runtime, and the user can refuse.
- **Special** permissions for powerful operations such as drawing over other apps, granted in a separate settings page.

Android's own best practices: request the minimum; "request permissions as late into the flow of your app's use cases as possible", tied to the action that needs them; remember that libraries you include bring their permission requirements with them.

blocks.title: Asking for the microphone at the moment it is needed (Kotlin)
blocks.code:
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml: declare only what a feature needs -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO" />

class VoiceNoteActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val askMic = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
    ) { granted ->
        if (granted) startRecording() else showWhyMicIsNeeded()
    }

    fun onRecordButtonClicked() {
        val state = ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(
            this, Manifest.permission.RECORD_AUDIO)
        if (state == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) {
            startRecording()
        } else {
            askMic.launch(Manifest.permission.RECORD_AUDIO)
        }
    }
}

scenes.caption: The manifest declares the one runtime permission this feature needs. Declaring is not granting: for a dangerous permission, nothing is allowed until the user agrees.
The app registers a callback for the permission result when the screen is created, but asks nothing yet. No prompt at launch.
The user taps Record. Only now does the app check the permission, because this is the action that needs it.
Not yet granted, so the system dialog appears. The user understands why: they just pressed Record.
If granted, recording starts; if refused, the app explains and keeps working without the feature. Checking every time matters: users can revoke permissions in settings at any moment.

blocks.md:
**Least privilege as a security control, not just privacy.** Every permission an app holds is something an attacker inherits if they compromise the app. A flashlight app with contacts and SMS access is a better target than one without. For defenders reviewing apps (in an enterprise app review, or a mobile assessment following the testing guide from OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, in lessons 14 and 15) the questions are: does each requested permission match a visible feature?
