Are dangerous ones requested in context? Do third-party SDKs (software development kits: libraries for advertising, analytics) pull in permissions or data the app's own features do not need?

**Platform enforcement.** Both systems let users review and revoke access per app in settings; apps must handle refusal. Android's **signature** level and iOS's signed **entitlements** cover capabilities a user should never be asked about, such as acting as a VPN or reading another app's data.

Android's special permissions guard 'particularly powerful actions', such as drawing over other apps, and are granted on the Special app access settings page rather than through a prompt. When checking a phone you suspect is being monitored (lesson 18), review that page as well as ordinary permissions.

blocks.question: A to-do list app requests location, contacts and microphone at first launch, before showing any screen. Which least-privilege principle does this violate most directly?
options: Request permissions late, tied to the specific user action that needs them, and only those a feature actually uses
All permissions must be install-time
Apps must use signature permissions
Apps must not use the internet
blocks.explain: Android's guidance is to request runtime permissions as late as possible, in context, and to request the minimum. A to-do list has no obvious need for any of these at launch, which is also a red flag in app review.

blocks.question: Why does an app need to check a runtime permission each time before using it, even if the user granted it last week?
options: It does not; one check is enough
Permissions expire every day
Users can revoke permissions in settings at any time, so a past grant does not guarantee current access
The check unlocks the Secure Enclave
blocks.explain: Android's documentation: don't assume permissions have been previously granted; check them before each access. Revocation is a user's control, and apps must handle it gracefully.

lessons.title: Mobile app storage: secrets on disk and in the package

blocks.md:
Platform security protects apps from each other. It does not protect an app from its own mistakes. The **OWASP MASVS** (Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, from OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project) is the industry checklist for those mistakes, with the **MASTG** (Mobile Application Security Testing Guide) explaining how to test each one and **MASWE** (Mobile Application Security Weakness Enumeration) naming the weaknesses.

Its storage category starts from the fact that apps keep sensitive data ("personally identifiable information (PII), cryptographic material, secrets, and API keys") on the device, sometimes in places other apps or the user can reach, and sometimes by accident through "backups or logs". Two controls: MASVS-STORAGE-1, "The app securely stores sensitive data", and MASVS-STORAGE-2, "The app prevents leakage of sensitive data".

Who can read an app's "private" files? Not other apps (lessons 11 and 12). But: anyone with the unlocked device and the right tools, a device backup, forensic extraction of a seized or stolen device, malware that gains root, and the app's own logs. Private storage is a good place for data that is not secret; it is not a safe for secrets. MASWE names the common failures, among them **MASWE-0001** sensitive data stored unencrypted in private storage, **MASWE-0003** cryptographic keys stored outside the platform keystore, and **MASWE-0004** sensitive data hardcoded in the app package.

blocks.caption: Kotlin, Android. Both mistakes pass every functional test; only a security review or a MASTG-style test finds them.

Kotlin, Android Keystore APIs. The Jetpack EncryptedSharedPreferences library was deprecated in 2025 'in favour of existing platform APIs and direct use of Android Keystore', which is what this does. AES-GCM is authenticated encryption (lesson 3): it encrypts and adds a tag that detects tampering.

blocks.title: What a backup or a rooted attacker finds in shared_prefs

scenes.caption: Vulnerable version: the token sits in readable XML. Anyone who gets the file (backup, rooted phone, forensic copy) can replay it as the user.
Fixed version: the file holds an IV and ciphertext. Without the key they are useless.

The key is in the Android Keystore, outside the app process and, on most devices, in secure hardware (TEE, trusted execution environment: an isolated part of the processor). Copying the app's files to another device copies nothing that decrypts them.

blocks.caption: Swift, type-checked with swiftc. Per Apple's guide, keychain items are encrypted with keys protected by the Secure Enclave, and 'ThisDeviceOnly' items are bound to the device's UID key, so a backup restored elsewhere cannot use them.

blocks.md: Obfuscating a hardcoded secret (splitting it, XORing it, hiding it in native code) only slows an analyst down; the app must reconstruct it to use it, so an attacker with the app can too. If a value must stay secret from users, it must not be in the app.

**Defender view.** Prevent: decide per data item whether it needs to be stored at all; keep tokens short-lived; keys in the Keystore or Keychain; no secrets in the package; exclude sensitive files from backups; never log tokens. Detect: MASTG-style testing of your own builds: inspect the app's data directory on a test device after login, unpack the release package and search it for keys and URLs, read the logs during a session. Respond: a leaked hardcoded secret is a credential incident; rotate it server-side, because every installed copy of the app still contains it.

blocks.question: A banking app stores its refresh token in SharedPreferences with MODE_PRIVATE. The developer argues other apps cannot read it. Which threat does the argument miss?
options: Other apps on the same device
Backups, forensic extraction of a lost device, and malware with root, all of which can read the app's private files
The Play Store
Network attackers
blocks.explain: The UID sandbox does stop other apps. It does not stop someone who obtains the files by other routes. MASWE-0001 covers exactly this: sensitive data unencrypted in private storage.

blocks.question: Why is the Keystore-based fix stronger than encrypting the token with an AES key stored in the same SharedPreferences file?
options: Because SharedPreferences cannot store keys
It is not stronger
AES in the Keystore is a different algorithm
Because the Keystore key never enters the app process and cannot be exported, so copying the app's files does not copy the key
blocks.explain: Encrypting with a key stored next to the ciphertext only adds a step. The Android Keystore keeps key material outside the app's process (often in secure hardware) and enforces how it can be used, which is MASWE-0003's point.

lessons.title: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning

blocks.md:
Lesson 9 concluded that on hostile Wi-Fi, TLS with correct certificate validation is what protects you. Browsers get that right and show a warning when it fails. Apps are different: the developer writes the networking code, and there is no warning page. MASVS puts it this way: developers "may accidentally disable the platform secure defaults or bypass them entirely". Its controls: MASVS-NETWORK-1, "The app secures all network traffic according to the current best practices", and MASVS-NETWORK-2, "The app performs identity pinning for all remote endpoints under the developer's control".

Both platforms now ship safe defaults and a declarative file to adjust them. Android has the **Network Security Configuration** (an XML file referenced from the manifest); iOS has **App Transport Security** (ATS, settings in Info.plist).

**Android defaults** (from the Network Security Configuration documentation): for apps targeting Android 9 (API 28) and higher, the base configuration is `cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"` and trusts only the **system** CA store. Apps targeting Android 6.0 and lower also trusted the **user** CA store, where anyone with brief access to the phone, or a confusing "install this profile" prompt, can add a certificate. The file can also pin keys, add a private CA for one domain, and allow extra CAs only in debug builds through `debug-overrides`, which apply only when the app is marked debuggable, something app stores do not accept.

blocks.code:
<!-- Vulnerable: res/xml/network_security_config.xml in a release build -->
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="true">      <!-- plain HTTP allowed -->
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="system" />
            <certificates src="user" />                   <!-- user-added CAs trusted -->
        </trust-anchors>
    </base-config>
</network-security-config>

<!-- Fixed: HTTPS only, system CAs only, pinned API keys with a backup pin,
     and the user store trusted only in debuggable builds -->
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false">
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="system" />
        </trust-anchors>
    </base-config>
    <domain-config>
        <domain includeSubdomains="true">api.example.com</domain>
        <pin-set expiration="2027-06-01">
            <pin digest="SHA-256">7HIpactkIAq2Y49orFOOQKurWxmmSFZhBCoQYcRhJ3Y=</pin>
            <pin digest="SHA-256">fwza0LRMXouZHRC8Ei+4PyuldPDcf3UKgO/04cDM1oE=</pin>
        </pin-set>
    </domain-config>
    <debug-overrides>
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="user" />
        </trust-anchors>
    </debug-overrides>
</network-security-config>
blocks.caption: Both files validated with xmllint; the pin values are the documentation's examples. Android's docs advise always including a backup pin, and warn that a pin expiration date lets un-updated apps keep working but 'may enable attackers to bypass your pinned certificates'.

blocks.md: The configuration file only governs the platform's own TLS stack. A developer can still override certificate checking in code, often to make a test server with a self-signed certificate work, and then ship it. This is the most common serious mobile networking bug: a **trust manager** (the Java object that decides whether a certificate chain is acceptable) that accepts everything.

blocks.title: A trust-all app on hostile Wi-Fi, before and after the fix

scenes.caption: Simplified. The phone is on a hostile hotspot (lesson 9). The app opens a TLS connection to its API; the hotspot intercepts it and answers itself.
The proxy presents a certificate it made itself for api.example.com. No trusted CA signed it.
The trust-all code accepts it. The app sends the user's credentials into a TLS session that ends at the attacker, who relays them to the real API and reads everything.
Fixed app: default validation (and, here, a pin). The self-made certificate fails the chain check, the connection is refused, and nothing is sent.
On a trustworthy network the real server's certificate validates and the session is end to end.

blocks.caption: Kotlin. An empty checkServerTrusted never throws, so every chain 'passes'; the hostname verifier returning true accepts a valid certificate for any other site too. The fix is deleting code, not adding it.

blocks.code:
<!-- Vulnerable Info.plist: ATS switched off for every connection -->
<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
    <key>NSAllowsArbitraryLoads</key>
    <true/>
</dict>

<!-- Narrow exception: plain HTTP to one legacy host only, ATS everywhere else -->
<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
    <key>NSExceptionDomains</key>
    <dict>
        <key>legacy-cams.example.net</key>
        <dict>
            <key>NSIncludesSubdomains</key>
            <false/>
            <key>NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads</key>
            <true/>
        </dict>
    </dict>
</dict>
blocks.caption: Fragments of Info.plist, checked with plutil. Apple: ATS requires HTTPS with TLS 1.2 or later, forward secrecy and strong certificates, and setting NSAllowsArbitraryLoads to YES 'completely disable[s] ATS for all network connections'. Fix the server rather than add exceptions.

blocks.md:
On iOS the equivalent of the trust-all bug is a `URLSessionDelegate` that answers every server-trust challenge with `.useCredential` without evaluating the trust; the fix is again to delete the override and let the system evaluate. Apple notes that with ATS on you can no longer *loosen* trust evaluation that way, but you can tighten it, for example to pin.

**A platform bug, for contrast: goto fail (2014).** Sometimes the TLS library itself is wrong. Adam Langley of Google [explained](https://www.imperialviolet.org/2014/02/22/applebug.html) CVE-2014-1266 in Apple's SecureTransport: a duplicated `goto fail;` line skipped the check of the server's signature on the key exchange, so any server could present a valid certificate chain without proving it held the matching private key. Apple fixed it in iOS 7.0.6. App code could not fix that; only an OS update could, which is why device patch levels matter (lesson 16).

Leave certificate validation to the platform. The bug is almost always code that disables it: an empty trust manager, an always-true hostname verifier, a delegate that trusts any server, or a blanket ATS or cleartext exception. Pin only endpoints you control, and always ship a backup pin. Pins outlive app releases: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030, so plan rotation to post-quantum keys.

blocks.question: A tester installs a proxy's CA certificate in the phone's user certificate store, then sees an Android app's HTTPS traffic in clear. The app targets API 34 and has no network security config. What does that indicate?
options: The app's own code overrides validation (for example a trust-all trust manager or custom TLS stack), because the default config for API 28+ trusts only system CAs
The proxy broke TLS 1.3
The phone is rooted
Normal behaviour for all apps
blocks.explain: Apps targeting Android 7.0 (API 24) or later do not trust user-added CAs by default, and for API 28+ the default base-config also forbids cleartext. If a user CA is accepted, something in the app changed the default.

blocks.question: Why does Android's pinning documentation insist on a backup pin?
options: To allow user CAs
To double the encryption strength
Because if the pinned key must change (key rotation or a CA change), an app with only one pin cannot connect until users install an update
Because Android requires exactly two pins
blocks.explain: A pin is a hard rule in shipped code. If the server key changes and no other pinned key matches, every installed copy fails closed. A pre-generated backup key, pinned in advance, keeps you able to rotate.

lessons.title: Managing fleets: MDM, BYOD and SIM swap defences

blocks.md: An organisation with thousands of phones cannot configure each by hand. **MDM** (mobile device management) is the service that does it centrally: it pushes Wi-Fi and VPN profiles (lesson 5's CA and server-name settings), requires a passcode and encryption, installs and removes work apps, reports OS and patch versions, and can wipe a lost device. The harder question is ownership. On a company-owned phone the organisation can control a lot. On **BYOD** (bring your own device) the phone is the employee's, and both platforms now draw a line down the middle of it.

**Android work profile.** Since Android 5.0 a device can carry a **work profile**: in Android's documentation, a profile "controlled by an IT admin" whose functionality "is set separately from the functionality of the user's primary profile". The two profiles have separate storage, intents (Android's messages asking another app or component to do something, such as open a link) do not cross between them by default, and the admin chooses which apps exist in the work side.

**Apple User Enrollment.** Apple's account-driven **User Enrollment** is "designed for BYOD" where "the user, not the organization, owns the device". The organisation can apply "only a limited set of payloads and restrictions" and can manage "only an organization's accounts, settings, and information ... never a user's personal account". Organisations that need more control use Device Enrollment, and company-owned fleets use **Automated Device Enrollment**, set up through Apple Business or Apple School Manager.

blocks.title: One BYOD phone, two worlds

scenes.caption: The MDM server manages only the work side: apps, accounts, a VPN, Wi-Fi certificates. It can remove that side remotely, which is a selective wipe.
The personal side belongs to the employee. Under User Enrollment or a work profile, the organisation does not see or manage it.
Data does not flow across by default: separate storage, no shared intents. Leaks between profiles are a policy decision, not an accident.
What the organisation still needs: proof the device is patched and intact. The MDM reports the OS version and security patch level, and access to work data depends on it.

blocks.caption: Kotlin, simplified. A real compliance agent also checks attestation (for example Play Integrity) so a tampered device cannot simply report a fake date. The 90-day figure is an example policy, not a standard.

blocks.md: **MDM is also an attack surface.** A management profile can install CA certificates, VPNs and app restrictions, so a malicious or abusive enrollment is powerful. Apple's Lockdown Mode (lesson 18) blocks installing configuration profiles and enrolling in MDM while it is on, and Apple's Safety Check notes that some options may not be available when an MDM profile is installed; reviewing installed profiles is part of checking a phone you suspect.

**SIM swapping.** A **SIM swap** (persuading or bribing a mobile carrier to move a victim's number to a SIM, Subscriber Identity Module, that the attacker holds) defeats SMS codes: every code sent by text now reaches the attacker. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) 2022 [public service announcement](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2022/PSA220208) counted 1,611 SIM-swap complaints in 2021 with adjusted losses above USD 68 million, and lists the methods: social engineering, insider help, and phishing of carrier employees. The mobile-specific defences: a carrier account PIN or port-out lock; MDM-managed authenticator apps or passkeys instead of SMS for work accounts; and treating "my phone suddenly has no service" as a security alert.
Write down which corporate systems still accept SMS codes or SMS-based account recovery. Every one of them is reachable by a SIM swap that never touches the phone or your MDM.

blocks.question: An employee enrolls a personal iPhone through account-driven User Enrollment. Which action is outside what the organisation can do?
options: Configure the corporate Wi-Fi with a pinned CA
Read the user's personal iCloud photos
Remove its managed data
Install a managed work app
blocks.explain: Apple's design: with User Enrollment, IT can manage only the organisation's accounts, settings and information, never the user's personal account. Selective removal of managed data is in scope; personal content is not.

blocks.question: A help-desk policy lets users reset their VPN password with a code sent by SMS. Which attack does this expose, regardless of how well the phone itself is managed?
options: A SIM swap that diverts the SMS code to the attacker's SIM
BlueBorne
An evil twin
KRACK
blocks.explain: The attacker attacks the carrier, not the device: once the number moves, codes go to them. The FBI PSA describes exactly this use against account recovery. Move recovery to non-SMS factors.

lessons.title: Zero-click attacks: from Trident to the Pixel 9 chain

blocks.md:
Everything so far assumed the attacker needs something from the victim: proximity, a password, a click. **Mercenary spyware** (commercial surveillance tools sold to governments) aims higher. Apple's threat notification page describes such attacks as costing "millions of dollars", deployed against a very small number of people, "often journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats". The technical goal is a **zero-click** exploit chain: code execution from data the phone processes automatically, with no tap. Advisory level here: what was attacked, why it worked, how it was found and fixed.

Two terms. An **exploit chain** links several bugs, each crossing one layer from lessons 11 and 12: first code execution in a parser, then a **sandbox escape**, then the **kernel**, then an **implant** (the spyware that is installed and runs on the phone). **Zero-day** means the vendor did not know about the bug when it was used.

**2016, Trident: one click.** Ahmed Mansoor, a UAE human rights defender, received SMS messages promising "new secrets" about detainees. Instead of clicking, they sent them to the **Citizen Lab** (a research lab at the University of Toronto that investigates targeted surveillance), whose [report](https://citizenlab.ca/2016/08/million-dollar-dissident-iphone-zero-day-nso-group-uae/) with the security firm Lookout found three iOS zero-days: a Safari (WebKit) bug for code execution from a web page, a bug that disclosed kernel memory, and a kernel bug for code execution, together a remote **jailbreak** (removing iOS's restrictions so the attacker's code runs with full control) that would have installed **Pegasus** spyware from NSO Group, an Israeli company that sells surveillance tools to governments.

**2019, WhatsApp: a missed call.** Meta's [advisory](https://www.facebook.com/security/advisories/cve-2019-3568) for CVE-2019-3568: a buffer overflow in WhatsApp's VoIP (voice over IP, internet calling) stack "allowed remote code execution via specially crafted series of RTCP packets sent to a target phone number". Citizen Lab, helping WhatsApp identify victims, [found](https://citizenlab.ca/2019/10/nso-q-cyber-technologies-100-new-abuse-cases/) over 100 cases of abusive targeting of human rights defenders and journalists in at least 20 countries. RTCP (the RTP Control Protocol) carries control messages alongside a call's audio, and call setup runs before anyone answers: parsing without a click.

**2021, FORCEDENTRY.** Citizen Lab found files named `.gif` in the iMessage attachments of a Saudi activist's phone; they were really Adobe PSD and PDF files, and the PDFs carried the exploit. Apple patched CVE-2021-30860 on 13 September 2021 (iOS 14.8). Ian Beer and Samuel Gross of Project Zero later explained the path: iMessage passed anything ending in `.gif` to IMTranscoderAgent, *outside* BlastDoor, where the image library guessed the real format from the content, putting "over 20 image codecs" in reach. NSO targeted an integer overflow in the **JBIG2** decoder (a 1990s compression format for black-and-white scans) and used JBIG2's bit operations, over 70,000 segment commands, to build a small computer inside the decoder that ran the next stage. Apple then restricted the formats reachable there and moved GIF decoding into BlastDoor.

**2023, [Operation Triangulation](https://securelist.com/operation-triangulation/109842/).** Kaspersky, a Russian security company, noticed suspicious traffic from staff iPhones on its own corporate Wi-Fi. A four-zero-day iMessage chain began with an attachment exploiting an undocumented TrueType font instruction (CVE-2023-41990) and ended by writing to unknown hardware registers, unused by Apple's own firmware, to bypass the kernel memory protection called PPL (Page Protection Layer, CVE-2023-38606). The implant deleted the original message and had no persistence: devices could be reinfected after reboot.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a zero-click chain (concept level)

scenes.caption: Step 1: something arrives that the phone processes on its own: an iMessage attachment (FORCEDENTRY, Triangulation), call-setup packets (WhatsApp 2019), an audio message (Pixel 9).
Step 2: a memory-safety bug in that parser gives code execution, but only with the parser's privileges: a sandboxed, low-rights process if the platform is designed well.
Step 3: a second bug, often in the kernel or a driver the sandbox can still reach, escapes to full control. Fewer reachable drivers means fewer usable bugs.
Step 4: the implant reports to its C2 (command and control) server. Triangulation's implant cleared the original message and did not survive a reboot.
Every hop is a place to stop it: fewer auto-parsers, memory-safe parsing, tighter sandboxes, unreachable drivers, crash throttling, fast patches. Defenders raise the number of bugs a chain needs.

blocks.md: **2026, the Pixel 9 chain, from defenders.** In January 2026 Google Project Zero published a working zero-click chain against Google's own Pixel 9, partly to answer doubts about whether such bugs are exploitable. Natalie Silvanovich, a Project Zero researcher, explained the entry point: Google Messages now decodes incoming SMS and RCS (Rich Communication Services, the successor to SMS) audio attachments for AI transcription "with no user interaction", so audio decoders became zero-click surface. A bug in the Dolby Unified Decoder (CVE-2025-54957) gave code execution in the `mediacodec` sandbox; a bug in the BigWave driver, reachable from that sandbox (CVE-2025-36934), gave the kernel. Two bugs were enough. Project Zero's lessons: the decoder process on the Pixel 9 lacked the seccomp policy AOSP specifies; they could not exploit the same Dolby bug on iPhone or Mac, where it was compiled with a bounds-checking compiler flag; and the fix took long to arrive. Reported to Dolby on 26 June 2025, it reached Pixel users on 5 January 2026.

**Basebands.** The **baseband** is the separate processor running the cellular modem's own firmware. In 2023 Project Zero [reported](https://googleprojectzero.blogspot.com/2023/03/multiple-internet-to-baseband-remote-rce.html) four Samsung Exynos modem bugs allowing "Internet-to-baseband remote code execution" needing only the victim's phone number; until patched, turning off Wi-Fi calling and VoLTE (Voice over LTE) removed the exposure.

Zero-click attack surface is every parser that runs on attacker-supplied data before the user acts. New convenience features (previews, transcription, search) add parsers. Defence is architectural: fewer and memory-safe parsers, tight sandboxes, unreachable drivers, and short patch times.

**Detection and response.** Kaspersky found Triangulation through network monitoring of its mobile Wi-Fi and then analysed device backups with **MVT**, the [Mobile Verification Toolkit](https://docs.mvt.re/en/latest/), released by Amnesty International's Security Lab in July 2021 alongside its Pegasus forensic methodology. MVT parses iOS backups and Android data for known indicators of compromise; its own documentation warns that public indicators "are insufficient to determine that a device is clean". Practical steps for people at risk: update immediately (most of these chains were fixed in emergency updates); reboot regularly (Triangulation's implant did not survive one); take Apple's [threat notifications](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102174) seriously; get expert help; consider Lockdown Mode (lesson 18).

blocks.question: Why did the Pixel 9 chain need only two bugs while iPhone zero-click chains like Triangulation needed four or more?
options: Two-bug chains are impossible on iOS
The Pixel used WEP
Android has no sandbox
On the Pixel 9 the decoder's sandbox could reach a vulnerable driver directly and lacked the AOSP seccomp policy, so one escape bug reached the kernel
blocks.explain: Project Zero's part 3: few bugs were needed because the mediacodec context could reach the BigWave driver and the expected seccomp policy was missing. Longer chains are a sign of effective sandboxing; their recommendation was to reduce what media processes can reach.

blocks.question: A journalist's iPhone gets an Apple threat notification. Which first response best matches the guidance in this lesson's sources?
options: Install an antivirus app from the App Store
Ignore it; zero-click attacks leave no traces
Update the OS, seek expert forensic help (MVT-based analysis by Amnesty's Security Lab or a similar helpline), consider Lockdown Mode, and do not rely on a public-indicator scan alone
Factory reset immediately and discard all backups
blocks.explain: Apple says its notifications are high-confidence alerts to take very seriously. MVT's maintainers warn public indicators alone cannot show a device is clean and point to expert help. Wiping first would destroy the evidence analysts need.

lessons.title: Lockdown Mode, stalkerware and tracker abuse

blocks.md:
Lesson 17 ended with a choice for people at the highest risk: give up features to cut attack surface. Apple's **Lockdown Mode** (iOS 16 and later, macOS Ventura and later) is that trade made into a switch, "an optional, extreme protection" for "the very few individuals" personally targeted by sophisticated threats. With it on, per Apple's support page:
- **Messages**: most attachment types are blocked except certain images, video and audio; links and link previews are unavailable.
- **Web browsing**: certain complex web technologies are blocked.
- **FaceTime**: incoming calls from people you have not called in the last 30 days are blocked.
- **Wireless**: the device will not automatically join non-secure Wi-Fi networks, and 2G and 3G cellular support is turned off.
- **Device connections**: accessories and computers need the device unlocked.
- **Configuration profiles** cannot be installed and the device cannot be enrolled in MDM.

Read the list against lesson 17: it removes exactly the automatic parsers (attachments, previews, fonts, web features) and unsolicited channels that zero-click chains enter through. Android has an opt-in **Advanced Protection** mode too; Project Zero's Pixel post notes that on Pixel 8 and later, hardware memory tagging (MTE, Arm's Memory Tagging Extension, which catches many memory-safety bugs) is enabled only for users who opt into it.

**Stalkerware: the attacker close to home.** The opposite end of the threat spectrum is not a government but someone close to the victim. The Coalition Against Stalkerware (founded in November 2019) defines **stalkerware** as tools ("software programs, apps and devices") that "enable someone to secretly spy on another person's private life via their mobile device", monitoring messages, location, photos and calls while running hidden. The Coalition describes it as facilitating abuse such as partner surveillance and domestic violence: the attacker is usually someone close to the victim, not a remote hacker. The defences are the ones in this course, used deliberately: a passcode no one else knows, reviewing installed apps, special app access (lesson 13), configuration profiles and MDM enrollment (lesson 16), and account sessions.

Apple's **Safety Check** (Settings, Privacy and Security, Safety Check, iOS 16 and later) lets a person review and stop sharing with people and apps, reset system privacy permissions and review devices on their account; its Emergency Reset stops all sharing at once. Apple's guide puts safety planning first: "Before making changes or deleting information, consider potential impacts to your safety and privacy", because an abuser may notice that monitoring stopped.

**Item trackers.** Bluetooth trackers such as AirTag (lesson 10's BLE at work) let owners find keys and bags by having nearby phones relay the tracker's location. Slipped into someone's bag, the same device tracks a person. The defence is detection by the victim's own phone. In May 2024 Apple and Google shipped cross-platform alerts based on a joint specification, **Detecting Unwanted Location Trackers** (DULT), now being standardised at the IETF: iOS 17.5 and Android 6.0+ devices alert when an unknown compatible tracker "is seen moving with them over time".

The IETF accessory draft describes the mechanics a tracker must follow:
- It advertises a **near-owner** state when its owner's device is close by, and must switch to **separated** after it has been away from the owner for more than 30 minutes; alerts are suppressed only in near-owner mode.
- It advertises at least every 4 seconds, so detection works.
- Its Bluetooth address rotates and looks random, so passers-by cannot track the *owner*; the victim's phone therefore watches for a separated tracker that keeps reappearing near them.

blocks.title: How a planted tracker becomes an alert (simplified)

scenes.caption: Minutes 0 to 20: the tracker is with its owner, advertising near-owner mode. Phones that hear it do not alert.
Minute 20: the tracker is slipped into the victim's bag and the owner leaves. The draft requires a switch to separated mode after more than 30 minutes apart.
From minute 50 the tracker advertises separated mode. The victim's phone keeps hearing the same separated tracker as they move between places.
After the tracker has been seen moving with the victim over time, the phone alerts: '[Item] Found Moving With You'. The exact timing is set by each platform, so this point is illustrative.

blocks.md: **After an alert**, Apple's [support page](https://support.apple.com/en-us/119874) describes the options: play a sound on the tracker; use Precision Finding where supported; hold an NFC-capable phone to an AirTag to see its serial number and the last four digits of the registered owner's phone number (screenshot it as evidence); and follow the instructions to disable it, after which the owner stops receiving its location. Turning off Bluetooth or Location Services on your own phone "does not prevent the owner" from seeing the tracker's location; disabling the tracker does. If you feel unsafe, Apple advises going to a safe public place and contacting law enforcement, who can request owner information from Apple.

For someone being monitored by an abuser, every defensive step can also alert the abuser: monitoring stopping, a tracker going silent. Technical help here should follow the person's own safety plan, ideally with a domestic violence support service, not just maximise security.

**Practise legally.** Only on your own devices, your own networks, and platforms built for it:
- Decrypt the Wireshark project's sample WPA capture with its published passphrase, following [HowToDecrypt802.11](https://wiki.wireshark.org/HowToDecrypt802.11) and the [sample captures](https://wiki.wireshark.org/SampleCaptures) page, and find the four EAPOL handshake frames. It shows lesson 3's point: passphrase plus handshake equals plaintext.
- Audit your own home network: list your BSSIDs and their security modes, turn on WPA3 or WPA3 transition with PMF where your devices support it, and check router firmware.
- Work through the OWASP [MASTG](https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/) and its deliberately vulnerable [crackme apps](https://mas.owasp.org/crackmes/) to find insecure storage and broken certificate checks.
- Run MVT on a backup of your own phone using its [documentation](https://docs.mvt.re/en/latest/), and read the indicator lists it uses.
- Try the mobile and network forensics challenges on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/).

blocks.question: Which Lockdown Mode restriction most directly targets the zero-click entry points from lesson 17?
options: Most message attachment types are blocked and link previews are off, removing automatic parsing of attacker-sent content
Game Center is disabled
Location is removed from shared photos
Shared albums are removed
blocks.explain: FORCEDENTRY and Triangulation both entered through iMessage attachments parsed automatically. Blocking most attachment types and previews removes those parsers from the attack surface; the other restrictions serve privacy or other channels.

blocks.question: Why must a DULT-compatible tracker rotate its Bluetooth address, and how can detection still work?
options: Rotation saves battery; detection uses GPS
A fixed address would let strangers track the owner; the victim's phone instead watches for a tracker in separated mode that keeps appearing near it over time
Rotation hides the tracker from its owner
Detection requires the owner's permission
blocks.explain: The IETF draft requires a random-looking, rotating address to protect the legitimate owner's privacy. Unwanted-tracking detection relies on the separated-mode signal and on seeing it move with the person over time.

blocks.question: A person finds an unknown AirTag in their bag and turns off Bluetooth on their iPhone. Does that stop the AirTag's owner from seeing where it is?
options: No: other phones nearby still relay its location; Apple's guidance is to disable the tracker itself, with personal safety in mind
Yes, if Location Services is also off
Only on Android
Yes, AirTags need the victim's Bluetooth
blocks.explain: Apple's support page says turning off Bluetooth or Location Services does not prevent the owner from seeing the location. The tracker must be disabled following the onscreen instructions, considering the safety implications.
